activities.anchor: Serious algorithm design starts before code, with a disciplined sequence
activities.caption: put the design method in order
activities.name: ccDesignOrder

config.prompt: Put the design method in order:
items: Decompose — 'produce a merit list' becomes read → average → sort descending → output
Identify inputs, outputs and preconditions — what if the file is empty or a mark is negative?
Choose representations — parallel arrays for index lookup, records for stable sorting
Write the algorithm as pseudocode — sequence, selection, iteration
Translate — an error at this point costs a release cycle, not minutes
config.why: Errors get costlier the later they are caught: minutes at the drawing stage, a debugging session in tested work, a release cycle in shipped software.

config.prompt: Bubble sort on a million items does about n²/2 comparisons — roughly how many?
config.why: 500 billion — hours of work; the n log₂ n alternative does about 20 million, under a second.
config.context: The lookup side tells the same story: 20 comparisons against 500,000 for the same million items.

items.label: the first and last record of a file

activities.anchor: a column per variable, one row per iteration, recording every change
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the trace table that catches the classic bug
activities.name: ccTraceCloze

config.text: Trace the loop for marks 60, 40, 80: total starts 0, becomes 60, %%0%%, 180; count runs 1, 2, %%1%%; average printed as %%2%%/3 = 60. If the average is computed inside the loop, the trace shows three %%3%% averages in five seconds.
config.hint: Assertions, unit tests and formal verification are automated versions of the same question.

activities.anchor: the distinction between a theorem about the set and a fact about a member
activities.caption: true or false — what the halting wall actually forbids
activities.name: ccHaltingJudge

statements.s: The halting problem means we can never tell whether any program halts.
statements.why: Specific programs are routinely proven to halt — a bounded loop is trivial; what is impossible is a single procedure that decides every case.

statements.s: Vendors claiming 100% guarantees are selling past a theorem.
statements.why: No tool can ever detect all viruses, prove all programs bug-free, or optimise away all dead code — each reduces to halting.

statements.s: Turing's machine needed an infinite tape, a head and a finite rule table — and computes everything every later proposal could.
statements.why: The Church–Turing thesis: no effective procedure has ever escaped it.

statements.s: The wall is about individual instances, not the general method.
statements.why: The reverse: it is about the general method; individual instances are routinely decidable.

activities.caption: walk the expert's path on a hard problem
activities.name: ccRouteBranch

config.root: A delivery company asks you to plan journeys for 200 cities, exactly. Walk the expert's path.

start.text: First question: is this problem NP-hard — does finding fast seem to require searching exponentially many options?

choices.label: Yes — assume worst-case exponential and engineer around it
choices.feedback: The pragmatic position: theory sets the wall's shape, engineering finds its doors.

choices.label: No — it is in P, polynomial time
choices.feedback: Sorting, shortest paths, matrix multiply — n² or n³ stays civilised; just write the algorithm.

around.text: 200 cities: brute force is astronomies even here. What actually works?

choices.label: Exploit structure no worst-case analysis sees
choices.feedback: The Concorde code found the exact optimum for 85,900 cities in 2006 by doing exactly that.

choices.label: Approximate — a provable 2-approximation
choices.feedback: 2-approximation algorithms and integer programming handle the rest of industry daily.

poly.text: In P: doubling the input multiplies the work by a civilised factor — the 'easy' class where sorting and shortest paths live.

structure.text: Exact answers, real instances: structure — not miracle algorithms — is what makes the impossible routinely solved.

approx.text: Provable near-answers in guaranteed time: the industrial compromise when exactness is priced out of reach.

config.why: Assume worst-case exponential, exploit structure, approximate — theory sets the wall, engineering finds the doors.

activities.caption: pair each class with its residents
activities.name: ccZooMatch

config.prompt: Pair each class with its residents:

pairs.right: solvable in polynomial time — sorting, shortest paths, matrix multiplication
proposed answers verify fast — a filled sudoku, a timetable
games like generalised Go and chess are complete here — even checking a win may take exponential time
what quantum computers solve efficiently — Shor's algorithm puts factoring here

config.why: The only field that sets the security budget of the internet: Shor moved factoring, so cryptography migrates to post-quantum schemes.
